A moving threequel about the value of sticking together amidst letting go. Highlights include: showing Andy actually playing with his toys, the sad truth about the army guys going first, Buster, toddler attack, Totoro, the villain from Network as the villain, every thing with Michael Keaton as Ken and Jodie Benson as Barbie, the intense escape sequence, Spanish Buzz, the claw will save us, getting emotional watching Andy say farewell to all his toys, and the overall comedy and drama matching the maturation of Andy and the audience
I never bought the incinerator moment that is often hailed as one of the great Toy Story franchise moments, but things did get a little dusty at the final scene. Ken is pretty fun too. 🧸🧸🧸.5 / 🧸🧸🧸🧸🧸.

Plot: 3 stars Characters: 4 stars Ending: 5 stars Enjoyment: 4 stars The toys head to daycare as Andy gets ready to leave for college. I liked the daycare setting but for whatever reason, I think Lotso was just ok as a villain. While all my favs are in this one, it felt more disjointed, and the Woody/Buzz relationship was weaker. That ending where Andy plays with Bonnie will absolutely wreck your life though.

Toy Story 3 is a movie that has all of the potential to be the single greatest movie for kids ever, but throws most of its chances away by following a few of generic formulas that the previous two installments already solidified. The main characters in this movie are absolutely spot on and perfectly characterized: Woody's whole philosophy of not abandoning his child and whole skepticism and all the parallels to Lotso's well constructed story arc and lore were perfectly shown throughout the whole runtime, especially in the scene where the bear abandons the toys in the garbage dump for absolutely no reason. The last heartwarming sequence of the film, with the toys moving on from Andy's care onto Bonnie's hands and all of dynamics changing, perfectly encapsulates the movie's core message and serves to a perfect finale for a beloved trilogy. Lotso is a great villain, Pixar's best, per say, but his companions (for most part) serve only as plot devices. Different from the group of protagonists that have actual personalities and feel like characters we may love (although some, like Mr. Potato Head, may be a bit flanderized here), their redemptions feel unearned and unrealized, except for the Big Baby and Ken. And Spanish Buzz sucked. However, to be fair, these are just nitpicks. For a kids movie, it is not expected that it takes a dark direction or that it follows great dark philosophies, serving as a lesson to kids that "sometimes, to love is to let go", and accept new cycles (just like Kung Fu Panda 4 tries to do and fails miserably). The whole cinematography, roller coaster of emotions, voice acting, animation, character designs and overall plot are absolutely excellent and stunning, especially in the movie's highest point, which is the dumpster scene. A really, really great lesson on how to make a movie rich for children and extremely entertaining adults, simultaneously. But not enough for me to consider it as a full masterpiece, especially as it falls into comercial traps to try and sell itself more often (Spanish Buzz).

Tanta roba. Perfetta fine della trilogia, ora capisco lo scandalo che c’è stato all’annuncio del 4. Il film è molto maturo, ha molte componenti tristi e più di una scena da lacrime virili. La grafica diventa veramente assurda e nel finale la butta completamente di fuori. C’è una bellissima scena d’azione di 10 minuti all’inizio della seconda metà del film che fa il culo a moltissime scene d’azione di film seri. Una delle cose più belle della trilogia ma che qui viene fatta alla perfezione è che qualsiasi caratteristica di ogni giocattolo, anche la più stupida, viene resa utile nel film e ogni volta in maniera geniale. Il finale è perfetto e mi ha messo paura per ciò che mi aspetterà nel 4. Non ricordo nulla se non per poca roba e quella poca roba mi pone già molti dubbi.

I grew up with the Toy Story movies; when this film released, I too was in my last year of high school, preparing to leave home and go off to college, and that gives this film a real emotional kick. The prison breakout plot is good family-friendly adventure, and the furnace scene at the end is one the most diabolical moments in any kids movie ever.

Dare I say, my favorite of the franchise..? Part 1 has a special place in my heart, and comes very close, but I enjoy this one the most! I love the whole prison break kinda vibe at the daycare, it was always fun, but the emotional punch the ending brings is what makes it a masterpiece. Watching these toys literally face the furnace together, to then seeing Andy finally pass his literal childhood down to Bonnie is just incredibly devastating. It’s so perfect. It’s a sort of bittersweet look at what if feels like to grow up and let go.

“Authority should be derived from the consent of the governed, not from the threat of force.” - Barbie. Change is terrifying - to have to confront the idea of your comfort being threatened, something you’ve known and experienced being replaced with something new and frightening, it takes a lot to overcome it. The Toy Story series have been a lot of things - it’s been more than 30 years since the first one revolutionised animation and thy just released a new one, the fifth in a long line of critically and commercially acclaimed films, but none of them are as good as Toy Story 3; its not just about sentient plastic, but about love, growth, comfort, purpose, betrayal and the idea of moving on, and it’s constructed in a manner that is inexplicably beautiful because of its masterful script and direction. Out of the three films so far in the series (and from the ones that came after), Toy Story 3 is the most emotionally mature, mainly because of how well it deals with the aforementioned themes - in a manner that is not just easy for a child to understand, but also for an adult who grew up with these films to appreciate and love. What starts as a standard lost and found story that has become the standard operating procedure for these films quickly evolves into a full blown “heist-like” feature, supplemented with some of the most heart-rending sub plots you could find in a film that is supposed to be marketed towards children. The tonal consistency in the screenplay is astounding, because this film manages to be so many things without trying too hard to be - it’s sad, funny (cackling and giggling funny), intelligent and down-right moving. The film also draws strength from the fact that it holds one of the most outrageously well written villains I could imagine. Lotso is literally Dr Doom levels of machiavellian evil, and it’s shockingly good! This is a character who’s heart was torn apart and is so full of pain and resentment that he refuses to accept any kind of attempt at redemption, right until the very end - it’s all done so well that you fully understand why he is the way he is, but never sympathise or justify his actions because of how cruel he is. It’s fucking brilliant I tell you, way too brilliant for a children’s movie. At its core, Toy Story 3 is about change, and how some people are able to cope with it, and how some aren’t. There’s a reason this is called one of the greatest animated films of all time, and it’s a title that is truly warranted.

Toy Story 3 is a great conclusion to Toy Story series, you’ll see what I mean when I talk about the fourth film. Looking through the movie, the first thing is that this is mostly a prison break film, which is certainly a unique option but it’s done very well with the style change. The animation has gotten to a point where it is equivalent to real life, especially with all the grime the toys get and the incinerator with millions of moving trash pieces by physics. The characters are very good, with all the original cast returning, expect for Bo, who would have broke into a million pieces during most of this film. The new characters are just as good, we get Lotso, possibly the best of an original animated villain by Pixar besides Syndrome, then an specific Barbie and Ken, probably the best at teaching me about the Barbie line without watching all 37 animated movies by Mattel, Ken is voiced by Micheal Caine, so he’s a British Ken. Then for all of Bonnie’s toys, they all done well in the film, some interesting casting is Trixie being Mabel from Gravity Falls, and Mr. Pricklepants being voiced by the late-80s Bond, Dalton. I personally think the best part though is Andy throughout the film. I, myself, am growing up, and I can relate to Andy aging and giving his toys away to a new generation. The ending still does make me cry to this day, and that is telling on how impactful this movie is. If there is a series that should all get 5 stars together, I'll say this one may be a contender. I guess the only bad thing is that Disney bought the rights to the cymbal monkey toy and, even though they never use it ever besides this film, they will file a lawsuit against any film using the monkey toy like The Monkey. I guess this is what happens when Disney is a capitalist company owning a product line patent.
